name: Madam Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower

card.summary: Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower was an early-1900s scalp pomade sold to treat dandruff and scalp problems and to help hair grow fuller and longer.
card.aka: Wonderful Hair Grower, Walker's Hair Grower
card.note: Historical product; a sulfur and petroleum-jelly style pomade.

quick.overview:
Wonderful Hair Grower was the signature product of Madam C. J. Walker, who began selling hair-care products in 1905 and built one of the first large Black-owned beauty businesses. It was a pomade applied to the scalp for dandruff, scalp ailments and thinning hair.

It helps looks by addressing scalp health and hair fullness; Walker said she herself had suffered from scalp problems and hair loss. It was used within a system of shampoo, brushing and pressing combs.
quick.how: Applied to the scalp as a pomade as part of a routine with shampoo and brushing, promoted door to door by trained sales agents.
quick.risks: Historical hair-care products of the era were sometimes harsh on the scalp; no modern clinical trial of this formulation exists.

lead: Madam Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower was a scalp pomade created in the first decade of the twentieth century by Sarah Breedlove, who sold it as Madam C. J. Walker [1]. She had suffered from severe dandruff and hair loss, which the biography links to harsh cleansers, poor diet, illness and infrequent washing [1].

The product was part of a method that included shampoo, a hair-growth pomade, vigorous brushing and the use of heated iron combs [1]. Its goal was healthier scalp and fuller, longer hair, and it was sold through door-to-door agents and ads in African-American newspapers and magazines [1].

Walker's business became a major enterprise, with several thousand sales agents employed between 1911 and 1919 [1]. A competing entrepreneur, Annie Turnbo Malone, accused Walker of taking her formula, described as petroleum jelly and sulfur that had been in use for roughly a century [1].

chain: Scalp ailments such as dandruff addressed
angle.text: The pomade was sold to treat scalp conditions and encourage hair growth, so that users' hair looked fuller and longer. It was used with brushing and pressing combs as a styling routine.

infobox: Petroleum jelly and sulfur (per a dispute)

paras: Breedlove worked as a commission agent for Annie Turnbo Malone's Poro Company around the 1904 St. Louis exposition, then moved to Denver in July 1905 and began building her own line [1]. After her 1906 marriage to Charles Walker she used the name Madam C. J. Walker, with 'Madam' borrowed from French beauty pioneers [1].
In 1910 she set up headquarters in Indianapolis [1]. The company claimed to have trained nearly 20,000 women by 1917 and later expanded to the Caribbean and Central America [1].

Products came in tins bearing her image and were sold by trained agents and advertised in Black newspapers and magazines [1]. Competitors included Malone's Poro System and Sarah Spencer Washington's Apex System [1].

timeline.event: Walker moves to Denver and begins her own product line [1].
Marries Charles Walker and adopts the Madam C. J. Walker name [1].
